canonicalExplanation.summary: A real link is `<a href="…">` with text that names its **destination**. Anchors come with free powers: keyboard focus, Enter to follow, open in a new tab, copy the address, and correct announcements by screen readers. Link text like "click here" means nothing out of context, and a `div` with a click handler has none of those powers. Mark the current page in a menu with `aria-current="page"`.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
Screen-reader users can pull up a list of every link on a page. On many sites that list reads: "click here, click here, read more, read more". Useless! A link named Read the C arrays lesson communicates its destination without surrounding visual context. In this lesson you'll improve a navigation set so destinations and the current context are understandable — and learn why a clickable div isn't a link. ```predict {"question": "`
Courses
` — can a keyboard user open it?", "options": ["Yes, with Enter", "No — a div isn't focusable or activatable by keyboard"], "answer": 1, "why": "Only real links and buttons get focus and keyboard activation for free. Use `Courses`."} ```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Sections and landmarks**, **Files, folders and paths**, **Relative and absolute URLs**, and **Paragraph and inline meaning**.

sections.heading: The model: a real anchor with destination text
sections.body:
```html
  • C programming
  • Read the C arrays lesson
  • Read the C pointers lesson
``` | Anchor gives you | A clickable div doesn't | |---|---| | Tab focus and Enter to follow. | ✗. | | open in new tab, copy link. | ✗. | | announced as "link". | ✗. | | works without JavaScript. | ✗. | ```reveal {"prompt": "Link or button — how do you choose?", "answer": "Link: goes somewhere (a URL). Button: does something on this page (submit, open a menu, toggle)."} ```

sections.heading: Text that stands alone

includes: Use real anchors with descriptive, unique link text.
Mark the current page with aria-current and choose links vs buttons correctly.

outcomes: Improve a navigation set so destinations and current context are understandable.

examples.title: A link that says where it goes
examples.situation: A link named Read the C arrays lesson communicates its destination without surrounding visual context.
walkthrough: **Before:** a card's link said "Click here", relying on the card's picture to explain it.
**After:** `Read the C arrays lesson` names the destination in the link itself.
**Check:** open the screen reader's links list and read each link without surrounding visual context.
examples.result: Every link in the list tells users exactly where it goes.

examples.title: The menu that lost its place
examples.situation: A course menu highlights the current page only with a CSS class `active` on a `span` (not a link).
walkthrough: Screen readers can't tell which item is current.
The current item isn't a link, so the menu is inconsistent for keyboard users.
Fix: keep all items as links and add `aria-current="page"` to the current one; style it with `[aria-current=page]` in CSS.
examples.result: Users hear "current page" on the right item, and the menu behaves the same everywhere.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Any element with a click handler is automatically equivalent to an anchor.
misconceptions.correction: Only a real `<a href>` provides focus, keyboard activation, new-tab and copy-link options, link semantics and no-JavaScript behaviour. A clickable div has none of these unless you rebuild them all.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening predict, why couldn't the keyboard user open the div?

analogy.example: Link text is like **road signs**: "Airport 5 km" helps; a sign reading "This way" helps nobody who didn't see the map. A clickable div is a painted door on a wall — it looks like a door but doesn't open.
limitations: Signs are read in place; link lists are read out of context.
aria-current is the "You are here" marker on a map.

faded.prompt: For "A link that says where it goes", explain how the link named Read the C arrays lesson communicates its destination without surrounding visual context, and what a keyboard user can do with it.
expectedEvidence: Names the example "A link that says where it goes": a link named Read the C arrays lesson.
It communicates its destination without surrounding visual context.
It's a real anchor, so Tab and Enter work.
It reads clearly in a links list.

nearTransfer.prompt: Rewrite a card grid whose links all say "Learn more" for courses HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Mark HTML as the current page.
expectedEvidence: aria-current="page" on the HTML link only.

farTransfer.prompt: Audit a page's links list (screen reader or a bookmarklet). Fix every vague or duplicate link text and replace any clickable non-links with real anchors or buttons.
expectedEvidence: All link texts unique and descriptive.
No clickable divs remain; keyboard test passes.

remediation.explanation: Read each link's text alone, out loud. If you can't tell where it goes, rewrite it. Then Tab through the page: anything you can click but can't reach by keyboard is a fake link.
remediation.retryPrompt: Do both checks on "The menu that lost its place".

recap.summary: To improve a navigation set, use real `<a href>` links whose text names the destination on its own, mark the current page with aria-current="page", and use buttons for actions — never clickable divs.
retrievalPrompts: What does an anchor give you that a clickable div doesn't?
Why is "click here" poor link text?
How do you mark the current page?
